Come, Deepak, sit down and put that phone face down. I'm Ankita, and I'll tell you how I stopped doing what you're doing.
A few years ago, when prices were falling, I checked them at breakfast, at lunch and again at night. My stomach was in knots by evening, and I kept wanting to sell just to make it stop. My flatmate Meghna said, "You've been snapping at everyone."
That was the moment I saw it: the more I looked, the more I panicked. So I muted every market channel and picked one day a month, the first Sunday, to open the portfolio for half an hour.
The urge to act didn't vanish. But by the first Sunday it was smaller.

qa.q: Which day of the month did Ankita choose to look at the portfolio?
qa.a: Ankita chose the first Sunday of the month.

qa.q: What was Ankita feeling in the evenings when prices were falling?
qa.a: Ankita was anxious, with a knotted stomach and an urge to sell just to make it stop.

qa.q: Ankita muted market channels and chose one day a month. What did that choice help with?
qa.a: It reduced constant checking, which was feeding the panic, so the urge to act on impulse grew smaller.

qa.q: How did Meghna see Ankita's habit of checking prices?
qa.a: Meghna saw a flatmate who had become sharp and irritable with everyone, which is why Meghna said so out loud.

Bhupen worked night shifts at a call centre in Guwahati, and during the market fall his phone never left his hand. Between calls he refreshed his investment app, market channels and three groups that posted red charts. On bad nights he checked forty times. He slept badly, and twice he nearly sold everything at 4 am.
His flatmate Ayesha watched him check the app during dinner one weekend. "Does looking make it go up?"
He thought about it later on the bus home. "Every time I check, I get scared. When I'm scared, I want to do something. And the something is usually selling." The checking wasn't information. It was fuel.
So he made a rule: portfolio check on the first Sunday of each month, nothing else. He muted the market channels and left two of the groups. The first week his thumb kept reaching for the app out of habit. By the third week, the urge to sell had almost gone.

qa.q: How often did Bhupen decide to check the portfolio?
qa.a: On the first Sunday of each month.

qa.q: What did Bhupen realise on the bus, and how did it feel?
qa.a: He saw that checking made him scared and pushed him toward selling; seeing this was likely uncomfortable but freeing.

qa.q: What else could Bhupen do when his thumb kept reaching for the app?
qa.a: Move the app off his home screen or log out, so the old habit needs an extra step.

qa.q: How does Ayesha see Bhupen's checking?
qa.a: Ayesha sees it as pointless, asking whether looking makes it go up.

grounding: It shows an investor noticing that constant price checking feeds fear and urges to sell, then limiting checks to once a month and muting market channels.

In his shared flat in Bengaluru, Thomas noticed a pattern in March. Every time he checked his portfolio, which was about every hour, his chest tightened and he opened the sell screen. Twice he closed it at the last second. His colleague Mridul laughed when Thomas showed him his phone's screen-time report: two hours a day on market apps and channels.
That night Thomas worked it out on the balcony. "The price moves whether I look or not. Looking only changes me. And the more I look, the more I want to act, and my urges have been bad ideas."
So he set a rule: a portfolio check once a month, on the first Saturday, with a cup of tea. He muted two market channels, unfollowed the loudest accounts and moved the investment app into a folder on his last screen.
By April his time on market apps was ten minutes a week. The market was still wobbly. He wasn't.

qa.q: How much time a day was Thomas spending on market apps and channels?
How did Thomas feel each time he checked his portfolio?
qa.a: His chest tightened with anxiety, and he felt pulled toward the sell screen.

qa.q: What else could Thomas do if the monthly check itself makes him anxious?
qa.a: Go through it with a friend or a registered adviser and write down his reasons before making any change.

qa.q: How does Mridul react to the screen-time report?
qa.a: Mridul laughs, perhaps surprised at how much time Thomas was spending, which nudges Thomas to rethink.

grounding: It shows an investor reasoning that frequent price checks raise anxiety and impulses, then checking monthly and muting market channels to calm those urges.
